issues.body: The blurb still says the FILTER is proved over a live-store integer `without disclosing it`, while operand_enc is public and deterministically identifies one of only four shipped values (24, 25, 30, 42). A verifier can enumerate OPERAND_ENC and recover the selected witness. Related panel/E2E wording equates absence of the literal field value with hiding, but the E2E assertion only proves that 30 is not itself a public field; it does not test or negate dictionary disclosure through operand_enc. This is materially the same major finding as round 4.
issues.fix_hint: Replace the blurb and related panel/README/E2E claims with a precise statement: the raw digits are private circuit inputs, but the deterministic public operand_enc may reveal low-entropy values by enumeration. Adjust the E2E description so it asserts only that digits are not direct public inputs. If actual value hiding is required, use a hiding commitment with verifier-bound randomness and test the resulting disclosure model.
issues.title: Deterministic operand_enc still makes the hidden-value claim false

verdict.summary: Round 5 is stagnant: the round-4 disclosure-model defect remains at major severity. The wording was narrowed in ProofSummary to say the raw store value is not literally among the public inputs, but the tool-level blurb, comments, and E2E narrative still claim the value is hidden from or not disclosed to the verifier. operand_enc remains a deterministic public input selected from the four-entry shipped OPERAND_ENC table, so a verifier can enumerate that table and identify the witness. The browser test still checks only that the integer field 30 is absent; it does not address dictionary recovery through operand_enc. The research-track/external-audit caveat does not make this specific nondisclosure claim true.
